title: Disputes Are Won or Lost Before Anyone Files
summary: A dispute is a business problem with a legal clock attached. The dispute ladder moves a disagreement up through negotiation, escalation, a dispute board, mediation and finally arbitration or court, and every rung is cheaper than the one above it. The developer's job is to design the ladder into the contract and keep the record that wins on any rung.
body:
Mr Shabazz, most construction disputes are decided by what was written in the contract and on site months before anyone calls a lawyer. Design the ladder on day one, keep the record every day, and you rarely need the top rung.

Recall

Q. In a risk register, what is a trigger?

A. An observable event or measurement, agreed in advance, that tells the risk owner a risk is moving from possible to happening and that the planned response should start.

Q. What does a waiver of subrogation do?

A. It stops an insurer, after paying a claim, from suing another party to the project in the insured's name. It keeps project parties from suing each other through their insurers, and it must line up with the insurance policies themselves.

Q. Why does cultural intelligence matter when dealing with authorities and communities?

A. Because the same words can carry different weight in different places. Knowing local norms on hierarchy, directness and time lets you be understood and avoid giving offence that costs approvals.

Why this matters

A developer who runs his own projects will have disputes. Not because he is careless, but because a building is a long contract between people with different incentives, signed before anyone knows what the ground, the market or the weather will do. The question is never whether a disagreement will arise. It is whether it stays a disagreement, settled in a week by two people who understand the contract, or becomes a dispute that consumes two years, a large share of the profit and your attention.

Disputes also move money in ways that are easy to miss. Cash withheld by a contractor, a lender pausing draws because a lien appears, an investor asking why the forecast changed: each is a cost of a dispute, and none appears on a lawyer's invoice.

The dispute ladder

Plain English first. A dispute ladder is a sequence of steps, written into the contract, that a disagreement must climb before it reaches the most expensive forum. Each rung is slower, costlier and less in your control than the one below it.

A typical ladder, from the bottom:

  1. Negotiation between the people running the job, usually the project managers, within a short fixed period.
  2. Escalation to senior executives on each side who were not involved day to day and can see the commercial picture.
  3. A dispute board or expert determination: an independent person or panel, often appointed at the start of the project, who hears the issue quickly and gives a decision or recommendation.
  4. Mediation: a neutral helps the parties reach their own settlement. The mediator decides nothing.
  5. Arbitration or litigation: a final, binding decision by a private tribunal or a court.

The professional framing is that each rung exists to filter out disagreements that do not need the rung above. A good ladder has short, fixed time limits at each step, so it cannot be used to stall, and it says clearly whether work continues while the dispute is resolved. Most construction forms require the contractor to keep working and the owner to keep paying undisputed amounts. That single provision prevents a disagreement over one change order from stopping the whole site.

A worked example, hypothetical. A contractor claims 400,000 dollars for unexpected rock in the excavation. The project managers meet within 7 days and agree that rock was found, but not on quantity. That is progress: the issue has narrowed from whether to how much. Executives meet within the next 14 days and agree 250,000 dollars for the rock that is measured and recorded, leaving 150,000 dollars of disputed overbreak, meaning rock removed beyond the design line. The overbreak goes to the dispute board, which decides in 30 days on the surveys. Total cost: a few days of senior time and one board fee. The same claim taken straight to arbitration would have cost far more than 150,000 dollars to decide.

Say that out loud now.

Every rung is cheaper than the one above it. The ladder is there to stop disagreements, not to schedule them.

Dispute boards, mediation and the final forum

A dispute board is an independent panel, often one or three experienced construction professionals, appointed at the start of a project and kept informed with regular site visits. Because they know the job before any dispute arises, they can decide quickly and credibly. The FIDIC suites of international contracts, which you met in Week 77, use a standing board in their 2017 editions, called a Dispute Avoidance and Adjudication Board; verify the exact mechanism against the edition you sign. Whether a board's decision is binding immediately, binding unless challenged within a period, or only a recommendation depends on the contract, and in some places on statute.

Mediation is different. The mediator has no power to decide. Its value is that it puts decision-makers in a room with someone skilled at testing each side's case privately. It works best when both sides have enough information to value their position, which is why the record matters even at this rung.

Arbitration and court are the two final forums. Day 4 compares them properly. For now, the essentials: arbitration is private, chosen by contract, and decided by arbitrators the parties help select; litigation is public, decided by a judge, and available whether or not the contract mentions it. Both are expensive, slow and largely out of your hands once begun.

The clock: limitation periods and time bars

Two clocks run on every dispute. A limitation period is the time the law allows to start a claim in court or arbitration; once it expires, the claim is usually lost, however strong it was. A time bar is a contractual deadline for giving notice of a claim, often a short number of days after the event. Miss a contractual notice and you may lose the right to extra time or money before any lawyer is involved. The length of each depends on the jurisdiction, the type of claim and the contract wording; verify that against the primary source before you rely on it [unverified — confirm independently]. Day 2 shows what happens when nobody watches either clock.

How the best do it

On large international infrastructure projects, sophisticated owners commonly appoint a standing dispute board at contract award and pay it to visit the site through construction, whether or not anything is in dispute. The board reads progress reports, walks the site and hears small issues early, informally, before positions harden. The practice is widely reported to resolve most matters below the arbitration rung. A small developer can copy the principle at small cost: name an agreed independent expert in the contract, such as a senior quantity surveyor or engineer, with a fee schedule and a 21-day decision period, and agree in advance that technical disputes go to that person first.

Omar's Six-Lens Check

Tax. The tax treatment of settlement payments, damages and legal costs depends on what the payment is for; verify that against the primary source before you rely on it. Liability. The contracting entity carries the dispute; guarantees and personal undertakings can pull it up to you. Banking. Loan agreements often treat material litigation or liens as a default or a draw condition, so tell your lender early. Governance. Decide in advance who may start, settle or abandon a claim, and minute it. Estate. A pending claim is an asset or liability that must be documented for whoever inherits your interests. Exit. A buyer or lender will price an open dispute as a discount or demand an escrow, so unresolved claims cost you at sale.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is a contract with no ladder, or a ladder with no time limits, so every disagreement either festers on site or jumps straight to the most expensive forum. The control is a dispute clause reviewed by counsel before signing, with fixed periods at each rung, a named independent expert or board, and an express duty to keep working and keep paying undisputed sums.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner treats a dispute as a matter of who is right. Being right is necessary and not sufficient. A right claim with no notice, no records and no budget loses to a weaker claim that was properly documented and pressed in time.

Callback

In Week 66, Kema and JAX taught negotiation: interests versus positions, and your best alternative to a negotiated agreement. The dispute ladder is that idea built into a contract. Every rung changes each side's alternative, and the cheapest settlements happen low on the ladder, when both sides can still see that their real interest is a finished building, not a judgment.

Recap

A disagreement becomes expensive only if it climbs. Build a ladder with short, fixed periods: negotiation, escalation, an independent board or expert, mediation, and then a final forum. Keep working and keep paying undisputed amounts. Watch two clocks, the legal limitation period and the contractual time bar. Professional sign-off required: construction litigation or arbitration counsel.

Next: Ford, with Cole, on Failure Forensics: a composite claim that died on the calendar.
checklist: My contract has a written dispute ladder with fixed periods at each rung.
An independent expert or dispute board is named, with a fee schedule, before work starts.
The contract requires work to continue and undisputed sums to be paid during any dispute.
Every contractual notice period is entered in a diary the day the contract is signed.
Limitation periods for each likely claim have been confirmed by counsel.
I know who in my company may start, settle or abandon a claim.
My lender is told early about any material dispute or lien.
I value every claim in money and time before choosing a rung.
head: Field checklist
speak: A dispute is a business problem with a legal clock attached. Most of them are decided by what was written in the contract and recorded on site long before anyone files. So design a dispute ladder on day one. Project managers negotiate first, within a fixed number of days. Then senior executives who were not in the trenches. Then an independent dispute board or expert who knows the job. Then mediation, where a neutral helps you settle but decides nothing. Only then arbitration or court, which are final, expensive and out of your control. Each rung is cheaper than the one above it, so the ladder exists to stop disagreements, not to schedule them. Two clocks run throughout: the legal limitation period to start a claim, and the contractual time bar for giving notice. Miss either and a strong claim can be lost. And always keep working and keep paying undisputed amounts.
terms: Dispute ladder — the contractual sequence of steps, from negotiation to a final forum, that a disagreement must climb, each with fixed time limits.
Dispute board — an independent panel appointed early in a project, kept informed through construction, that decides or recommends on disputes quickly.
Limitation period — the time the law allows for starting a claim in court or arbitration, after which the claim is usually lost.

hostile.q: Your contractor is threatening arbitration over a 600,000 dollar claim. Why should I keep funding draws while that is open?
hostile.a: Because the contract keeps the job moving: the contractor must keep working and we pay only undisputed amounts. The disputed 600,000 dollars is outside the draws and covered by contingency plus a reserve I am holding. The claim is in the second rung of our ladder, with an independent expert decision due within 30 days. I will send you the claim summary, our valuation and the expert timetable this week, and I will tell you the day anything changes.

title: The Claim That Died on the Calendar: A Composite
summary: This is a composite example. An owner discovered leaking windows, spent two years in friendly talks with the designer and the contractor, and then found that the contractual notice periods and the legal limitation period had run. The claim was strong and worthless. Seven forensic steps show where the clock was lost.
body:
This is a composite example. A developer had a strong claim for a defective building envelope and lost it without a hearing, because two clocks ran out while everyone was being reasonable.

Recall

Q. What are the usual rungs of a dispute ladder?

A. Negotiation between project managers, escalation to executives, an independent dispute board or expert, mediation, and finally arbitration or litigation, each with fixed time limits.

Q. What is professional indemnity insurance?

A. Insurance that covers a designer or consultant against claims that their professional advice or design was negligent. Its terms, limits and claims-made basis decide whether there is money behind a claim against them.

Q. Why is a contractor's community relations plan part of the owner's risk?

A. Because neighbours, road closures and noise complaints can trigger stop-work orders or political pressure that delay the job, and the owner carries the delay cost whoever caused it.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, Cole joins me today because this is a legal failure with no villain. Nobody lied. Nobody hid a document. The owner, the architect and the contractor all behaved like decent professionals trying to fix a problem. The owner simply forgot that the law and the contract were counting days while the people were talking. The numbers are hypothetical round figures.

1. Timeline

A developer completes a 60-unit residential building. In month 4 after completion, residents report water entering at several windows during storms. In month 6, the contractor sends crews to reseal joints. In month 10 the leaks return. In month 12, the developer's own consultant reports that the window installation does not match the approved details and that the design itself omits a sill flashing at one wall type. Estimated repair: 1,800,000 dollars. Meetings continue for 18 months. The architect's insurer is notified informally by email in month 14. In month 30 the developer instructs lawyers. The lawyers advise that the contract's notice clause required written notice of defects within a fixed period, that the insurer's policy required formal notice of a claim, and that the limitation period for at least part of the claim may already have expired.

2. Key decisions

Three decisions mattered. Treating the first reseal as a fix rather than as the start of a claim. Holding meetings without written notices, because notices felt aggressive. And waiting until settlement talks had clearly failed before calling counsel.

3. Assumptions

The developer assumed the clock started when talks failed. In many systems it starts when the damage occurred or when it was discovered or ought reasonably to have been discovered, a principle called discoverability; how it applies, and whether a separate ultimate deadline exists, depends on the jurisdiction [unverified — confirm independently]. He assumed a friendly email was notice. Contracts and policies usually define notice precisely: in writing, to a named person, with stated content. He assumed the other side's willingness to meet meant it accepted responsibility. Meeting is not admitting.

4. Incentives

The contractor's incentive was to keep repairing small areas, which cost little and delayed any formal claim. The architect's incentive was to avoid a claim on his insurance record. The developer's incentive was to keep relationships warm for the next project and avoid legal fees. Every incentive pointed toward delay, and delay was the one thing that destroyed the claim.

Cole's point: in a dispute, time is not neutral. It always favours the party who would lose on the merits.

Say that out loud now.

In a dispute, time favours the party who would lose on the merits. I watch the clock, not the mood.

5. Warning signs ignored

The return of the leaks after the first reseal, which proved the problem was not workmanship on a few joints. The consultant's month-12 report naming a design omission, which brought the architect in as a separate party with a separate clock. The contractor's refusal to put anything in writing. And the insurer's silence after the informal email, which should have prompted a formal notice.

6. Point of no return

The point of no return was the expiry of the first contractual notice period, early in the story, and then the limitation period, somewhere around month 24 on the lawyers' cautious reading. Before those dates, one letter would have preserved everything: a written notice of claim and a proposal for a standstill agreement. A standstill agreement is a contract between the parties that pauses the limitation clock for a defined period so that talks can continue without anyone losing rights. Most sensible counterparties sign one, because the alternative is being sued to stop the clock.

7. Root cause

The root cause was not the defect. Envelopes leak, designs have gaps. The root cause was that no one owned the calendar. The owner had no register of claims and deadlines, so a strong claim worth 1,800,000 dollars became a negotiation from weakness, and finally a write-off funded from the developer's own reserves.

Cole's view: what a record would have looked like

A one-page claims register, opened in month 4, would have listed: the event, the date first noticed, the parties who might be responsible, the contract clause requiring notice and its deadline, the policy requiring notice and its deadline, counsel's view of the limitation period and the earliest possible expiry, and the action taken. Reviewed monthly, it would have made the month-12 report trigger two letters the same week: a formal notice to the contractor and a formal notice to the architect and his insurer, each enclosing the consultant's report.

What a good notice says

A notice is not a threat. It is a short, factual letter that does four things: it identifies the event and the date it was first noticed; it states which clause of the contract it is given under; it says, in general terms, what the owner expects, such as repair, payment or an extension of the warranty; and it reserves all rights, meaning it states that nothing in the continuing talks waives the claim. Send it to the person and address the contract names, by the method the contract names, and keep proof of delivery. A notice that is correct in substance but sent to the wrong address, or by email where the contract requires courier, can be argued to be no notice at all.

Hypothetically, the letter in this case would have run to one page and cost an hour of a lawyer's time. Compare that with a 1,800,000 dollar repair funded from the developer's own reserves.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is that goodwill substitutes for procedure, so deadlines pass during friendly talks. The control is a claims register reviewed monthly, formal written notice the moment a claim is possible, and a standstill agreement signed before any limitation date comes close.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner thinks sending a notice will damage the relationship. Professionals expect notices and send them routinely; a properly worded notice says the relationship is being protected by procedure. The second beginner's mistake is calling a lawyer only when talks fail. Call when the claim first becomes possible, ask for the deadlines, and keep talking.

Callback

In Week 77, LEX and Marco taught conditions precedent and time bars in standard contract forms: a right that exists only if notice is given on time. This case shows the owner's side of that lesson. The time bars we press on contractors run against us too, and the law adds its own clock on top.

Recap

A strong envelope claim was lost because talks ran past the contractual notice periods and the limitation period. Incentives on every side favoured delay. One formal letter and a standstill agreement would have preserved it.

Rule 81: The day a claim becomes possible, diarise its contractual notice period and its limitation period, and never let talks run past either deadline without a signed standstill agreement or a filed claim.

Next: Roman on The Money: what a dispute really costs, and how settlement value moves your returns.
checklist: I open a claims register the day a defect or disagreement first appears.
For each claim, I record the contract notice clause and its deadline.
I record insurance notice requirements for every party who may be responsible.
I ask counsel for the earliest possible limitation date, in writing.
I send formal written notice, to the named person, as soon as a claim is possible.
I propose a standstill agreement before any limitation date comes close.
I treat a repeat failure after a repair as evidence of a larger claim.
I review the claims register every month with my project manager.
head: Field checklist
speak: This is a composite case. A developer's new building leaked at the windows. The contractor resealed joints, the leaks came back, and a consultant then found both poor installation and a design omission. Repair: 1,800,000 dollars. Everyone was reasonable and the meetings ran for 18 months, with no formal notices, only an informal email to the architect's insurer. When the developer finally called lawyers, the contractual notice periods had passed and the limitation period for part of the claim may already have run. The claim was strong and worthless. Incentives on every side favoured delay, and in a dispute, time favours the party who would lose on the merits. The root cause was that no one owned the calendar. Rule 81: the day a claim becomes possible, diarise its notice period and limitation period, and never let talks run past either without a signed standstill agreement or a filed claim.
terms: Discoverability — the principle in many legal systems that a limitation period starts when damage was, or reasonably ought to have been, discovered.
Standstill agreement — a contract between disputing parties that pauses a limitation period for a set time so talks can continue without loss of rights.
Claims register — an owner's running list of possible claims with dates, responsible parties, notice clauses, deadlines and actions taken.

hostile.q: You knew about these leaks for two years. Why should my insurer pay a claim you never properly notified?
hostile.a: I accept the formal notice came late, and I will not argue the timing beyond what the record shows. What the record shows is that your insured attended every meeting, received the consultant's report in month 12, and received written notice of the defect by email in month 14. I am asking your counsel to review those documents against the policy's notice wording before you decide, and I am proposing a standstill agreement today so neither of us has to file while that review happens.

rule: Rule 81: The day a claim becomes possible, diarise its contractual notice period and its limitation period, and never let talks run past either deadline without a signed standstill agreement or a filed claim.

title: What a Dispute Really Costs
summary: A dispute costs far more than legal fees. It ties up cash, slows draws, consumes management time and delays the date your returns start. Roman shows how to put a single number on a claim, compare it with a settlement offer, and see what each choice does to IRR and to your personal balance sheet.
body:
A dispute is an investment decision. You spend money and time now for an uncertain recovery later, and the honest comparison is always net, discounted and risk-weighted against the offer in front of you.

Recall

Q. What was Rule 81?

A. The day a claim becomes possible, diarise its notice period and limitation period, and never let talks run past either without a signed standstill agreement or a filed claim.

Q. What is a performance bond?

A. A promise by a surety, usually an insurance or bonding company, to complete the contractor's work or pay up to the bond amount if the contractor defaults, subject to the bond's terms and notice conditions.

Q. What is a broker's role in deal sourcing?

A. To bring opportunities and counterparties to the developer in exchange for a fee, which means the broker's incentive is to close a deal, not necessarily to close the right one.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, a lender looks at an open dispute and sees three things: money that may never come in, money that may have to go out, and a borrower whose attention is somewhere other than the job. All three move the numbers you care about: cash, net operating income (NOI) once the building runs, the internal rate of return (IRR) on your equity, and the debt service coverage ratio (DSCR), which is the building's NOI divided by its loan payments. If you can price a dispute the way I do, you will settle more claims sooner and fight the right ones harder.

The four costs nobody puts on the invoice

Legal and expert fees are the visible cost. Four others usually matter more.

  • Cash locked up. Money withheld by the other side, or money you must hold in reserve, earns nothing and may cost interest.
  • Delay to the return. If a dispute delays completion, sale or refinance, every dollar of profit arrives later, and IRR is very sensitive to timing.
  • Financing friction. Lenders may pause draws, require reserves or decline to refinance until a material claim is resolved.
  • Management time. A developer running a dispute is not finding the next site. That opportunity cost is real even though no one bills it.

Plain English: a 1,000,000 dollar claim that takes three years and 300,000 dollars of fees to win is not worth 1,000,000 dollars. The professional framing is that a claim has an expected value: the probability-weighted recovery, less costs, discounted to today for time and for the risk of not collecting.

A worked example: settle or fight

Hypothetical. A contractor owes you, on your best view, 1,000,000 dollars for defective work. It offers 550,000 dollars now. Counsel estimates a 70 percent chance of winning at arbitration, an award of about 900,000 dollars if you win, because tribunals rarely award every line, and 250,000 dollars of fees and expert costs, of which you might recover half if you win. Arbitration takes 2 years. You discount at 10 percent a year, your cost of equity.

  1. Expected award: 0.70 times 900,000 dollars equals 630,000 dollars.
  2. Expected cost recovery: 0.70 times 125,000 dollars equals 87,500 dollars.
  3. Expected gross recovery: 630,000 plus 87,500 equals 717,500 dollars.
  4. Discount two years at 10 percent: 717,500 divided by 1.21 equals about 593,000 dollars.
  5. Subtract fees, spent mostly over the two years, say 230,000 dollars in today's money: about 363,000 dollars.
  6. Collection risk: if there is a 20 percent chance the contractor cannot pay an award, multiply the recovery part by 0.8: about 474,000 dollars recovered, less 230,000 dollars of fees, gives about 244,000 dollars.

The 550,000 dollar offer today beats the expected value of fighting, before counting management time and financing friction. That does not mean you take it. It means 550,000 dollars is above your walk-away, and you negotiate from there with a clear number.

Say that out loud now.

A claim is worth its probability-weighted recovery, less costs, discounted for time and for the risk of not collecting.

What it does to the deal

Now look at IRR. Hypothetically, your equity is 5,000,000 dollars and the project was forecast to return it with a profit of 2,000,000 dollars at sale in year 3. A defect means 1,000,000 dollars of repair spent now. If you settle for 550,000 dollars this year, the net cost is 450,000 dollars and the sale stays on time. If you fight, you carry the full 1,000,000 dollar repair, plus fees, and a buyer insists on an escrow from the sale proceeds until the award is collected, so part of your profit arrives two years late. Even if you eventually win, the delayed cash can cost several points of IRR, because IRR punishes late money far more than the equity multiple does. Run both cases through your model; the difference is often the decision.

For DSCR, the effect is indirect but real. If repairs are funded from operating cash or a lender requires a reserve, the cash available after debt service shrinks, and a building close to its covenant can breach it. Week 36 taught that a covenant breach can turn a small problem into a lender's problem.

Warrick's Wealth Ledger

On your personal balance sheet, an open dispute belongs in two places. If you have guaranteed the project's obligations, a claim against the company is a contingent liability of yours: a debt that exists only if an event happens, which you should write down at a realistic estimate, not zero. And a claim you are pursuing is a contingent asset, which you should carry at its expected net value, never at its face amount. The habit protects your liquidity floor, the minimum cash you keep regardless of opportunity. A licensed adviser is required before you act on any personal financial decision.

A second example: the price of withheld money

Hypothetical. An owner withholds 300,000 dollars of the contractor's retainage, the percentage of each payment held back until completion, because of disputed defects. The contractor answers by slowing its punch list, the final list of minor items to finish. The building's opening slips 2 months. If the stabilised building is forecast to earn 1,200,000 dollars of NOI a year, two months of delay costs about 200,000 dollars of lost NOI, plus two months of construction loan interest. On a 20,000,000 dollar loan at 7 percent, that is roughly 233,000 dollars. The owner has spent about 433,000 dollars to protect 300,000 dollars.

The lesson is not that owners should never withhold. Retainage exists for a reason. It is that the decision to withhold must be priced against the cost of the reaction it provokes, and that holding back only the value of the disputed items, documented line by line, usually keeps the job moving where holding everything stops it.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is valuing a claim at its face amount, so you reject a sensible settlement and spend years chasing a number that was never real. The control is a written claim valuation, updated at each rung of the ladder, with probability, quantum, costs, time and collection risk stated separately.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner counts the money in dispute and forgets the time. Two years is not a pause in an investment; it is a cost, and on a development it can be the largest cost of all.

Callback

In Week 15, Sage taught that IRR is driven by timing as much as by profit, and that a refinance can manufacture an attractive IRR. Disputes work the other way: they push cash later, and a profitable project can deliver a mediocre IRR because one claim held back the exit.

Recap

Price every dispute as an investment: probability times quantum, plus expected cost recovery, discounted for time, adjusted for collection risk, less fees. Compare that with the settlement offer, then add the costs no invoice shows: locked cash, delay, financing friction and your time. Carry claims and exposures on your personal balance sheet at expected values.

Next: LEX on The Rules: arbitration versus courts, limitation periods and enforcement across borders, with Canada and Guyana compared.
checklist: I value every claim as probability times award, less costs, discounted for time.
I adjust every recovery for the risk that the other side cannot pay.
I count locked cash, delay, financing friction and management time as costs.
I run settle and fight cases through the project's IRR model.
I check whether a dispute threatens a DSCR covenant or a draw condition.
I set a walk-away number before every settlement conversation.
I carry guaranteed exposures as contingent liabilities on my personal balance sheet.
head: Field checklist
speak: A dispute is an investment decision. Legal fees are only the visible cost. The bigger ones are cash locked up, delay to your return, lenders pausing draws or refinancing, and your own time. So price a claim the way a lender would. Take the chance of winning times the realistic award, add the costs you might recover, discount it for the years it will take, cut it again for the risk the other side cannot pay, and subtract the fees. In my example a 1,000,000 dollar claim came out at roughly 244,000 dollars of net value against a 550,000 dollar offer today. That does not mean take the offer. It means you know your walk-away. Then run both cases through the IRR model, because delay hurts IRR more than profit does. On your own balance sheet, carry guarantees as contingent liabilities and claims at expected value, never face value.
terms: Expected value of a claim — the probability-weighted recovery, less costs, discounted for time and adjusted for the risk of not collecting.
Collection risk — the chance that a party who loses a dispute cannot or will not pay the award or judgment.
Contingent liability — an obligation that becomes real only if a future event happens, such as a guarantee being called.

hostile.q: You turned down 550,000 dollars to chase a million. Walk me through why that was a good use of my equity.
hostile.a: I did not turn it down; I used it to set my walk-away. Our valuation, at a 70 percent chance of winning, a 900,000 dollar award, two years and collection risk, came out well below 550,000 dollars net, so the offer sits above my floor. I countered at 700,000 dollars with the expert's report attached, and my authority is to settle anywhere above 550,000 dollars. The written valuation and the counter are in the board pack.

title: Arbitration, Courts, Clocks and Crossing Borders
summary: Arbitration and litigation are the two final forums, and the contract largely decides which you get. LEX compares them on privacy, choice of decision-maker, cost, appeal and, most importantly, enforcement across borders. Then the limitation clock, and a conceptual comparison of Canada and Guyana.
body:
Choose the final forum when you sign, not when you fight, and choose it by one question above all: if I win, can I collect, in the country where the other side's money is?

Recall

Q. Why is a claim worth less than its face amount?

A. Because recovery is uncertain, takes time, costs fees and may not be collectable. Its value is the probability-weighted recovery, less costs, discounted for time and collection risk.

Q. What is consequential loss in a construction contract?

A. Indirect loss flowing from a breach, such as lost profit or lost rent, as opposed to the direct cost of putting the work right. Contracts often exclude or cap it, and the meaning of the words used is itself a common dispute.

Q. What should a developer check before accepting a deal from a broker?

A. Who pays the broker and when, whether the broker represents the other side as well, and whether the opportunity has been shopped to others, because each changes the broker's incentive.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, a cross-border developer is exactly the person for whom this choice matters most. Your counterparty may be a contractor incorporated in one country, owned from another, with assets in a third. A judgment from a court in your country may be difficult to enforce where its money is. An arbitral award may travel more easily. The dispute clause is the single line in a construction contract that decides whether a win is worth anything.

Arbitration and litigation compared

Plain English: litigation is a claim decided by a state court under that court's procedures. Arbitration is a claim decided by private arbitrators, appointed under rules the parties chose, and it happens only because the contract says so.

The professional framing compares them on six points.

  • Privacy. Court proceedings are usually public. Arbitration is usually private, and often confidential by agreement or by the rules chosen.
  • Decision-maker. In court you get the judge assigned. In arbitration the parties usually help choose the arbitrators, and can choose people with construction expertise.
  • Procedure. Courts follow fixed rules. Arbitration follows the chosen institutional rules, adapted by the tribunal, which can be faster or slower in practice.
  • Cost. In arbitration the parties pay the arbitrators and the institution as well as their lawyers. It is not reliably cheaper.
  • Appeal. Court judgments can usually be appealed. Arbitral awards are usually final, with very limited grounds to challenge them, which is a strength and a risk.
  • Enforcement. The decisive point for cross-border work, below.

What a good arbitration clause names

An arbitration clause must say enough to work without a further agreement between people who are, by then, in dispute. At minimum it names: the seat, which is the legal home of the arbitration and decides which country's courts supervise it; the rules, usually an institution's published rules; the number of arbitrators, one or three; the appointing method; the language; and the governing law of the contract, which is a separate question from the seat. Arbitration clauses are commonly treated as separate from the rest of the contract, a principle called separability, so a claim that the contract is invalid can itself be arbitrated; verify that against the law of the seat before you rely on it.

A worked example, hypothetical. A developer signs a 30,000,000 dollar contract with a foreign contractor whose assets are outside the developer's country. Clause one: disputes go to the courts of the developer's country. Clause two: disputes go to arbitration under named institutional rules, three arbitrators, seated in a neutral country that recognises foreign awards, in English. If the developer wins 2,000,000 dollars under clause one, he may need a fresh proceeding in the contractor's country to have the judgment recognised, and the outcome depends on that country's law and any treaty between the two. Under clause two, if both countries are parties to the convention described below, the award can usually be enforced through a simpler recognition process, subject to narrow defences.

Say that out loud now.

If I win, can I collect, in the country where the other side's money is? That question chooses the forum.

Enforcement across borders

The main instrument for arbitral awards is the 1958 Convention on the Recognition and Enforcement of Foreign Arbitral Awards, usually called the New York Convention. Countries that are parties to it agree to recognise awards made in other member countries, refusing only on limited grounds such as a party not having had a proper chance to present its case, or enforcement being contrary to public policy. Many countries are parties; check whether each country involved in your deal is, and on what terms, before relying on it [unverified — confirm independently]. There is no equally broad instrument for court judgments, so recognition of a foreign judgment usually depends on the receiving country's own rules or on specific treaties.

Two practical points. First, enforcement is against assets, so know where the counterparty's assets are before you sign. Second, a parent company guarantee or a bank letter of credit, which you met in Week 79, can make enforcement unnecessary: you call the security rather than chase a judgment.

Limitation periods, conceptually

Every system sets time limits for starting a claim. They differ by type of claim, such as contract, negligence or a claim on a deed, and many include a discoverability rule and an ultimate long-stop after which no claim can start whatever was known. Contracts can sometimes shorten or lengthen them within limits the law allows, and a standstill agreement can pause them. Never assume a number. Verify that against the primary source before you rely on it [unverified — confirm independently].

Two Systems: Canada and Guyana

This is a conceptual comparison; verify against primary source before relying on any point. In Canada, most provinces have modern arbitration statutes, and international commercial arbitration is commonly governed by legislation based on the United Nations model law; Canada is a party to the New York Convention, and limitation periods are set by provincial statute, often with a basic period running from discovery and an ultimate period, with Quebec's civil law applying its own rules. In Guyana, the legal system is rooted in English common law, arbitration is governed by statute, and limitation of actions is also statutory; whether and on what terms Guyana is a party to the New York Convention, and how foreign judgments are recognised, should be confirmed directly [unverified — confirm independently]. In both, the practical answer is the same: name the seat and the rules precisely, know where the assets are, and diarise the clock.

Professional sign-off required: litigation and arbitration counsel admitted in each relevant jurisdiction.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is a dispute clause that produces a decision you cannot enforce where the money is, or one so vague, sometimes called pathological, that the parties must litigate about where to litigate. The control is a clause drafted by arbitration counsel, naming seat, rules, number of arbitrators, appointment, language and governing law, checked against the counterparty's asset location.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner copies a dispute clause from the last contract. The right forum depends on who the counterparty is and where its assets sit. A clause that suited a local contractor can be useless against a foreign one.

Callback

In Week 19, LEX taught sources of law and the difference between common law and civil law systems. Enforcement is where that lesson turns into money: an award or judgment is only paper until a court in the asset's country agrees to act on it, under its own law.

Recap

Litigation is public, appealable and assigned; arbitration is private, chosen, usually final and often easier to enforce abroad through the New York Convention. A working arbitration clause names seat, rules, arbitrators, appointment, language and governing law. Limitation periods vary by system and claim type and must be verified, never assumed.

Next: Quincy on The Numbers: valuing a delay claim and a settlement offer, step by step.
checklist: I choose the final forum by asking where the counterparty's assets are.
My arbitration clause names the seat, rules, number of arbitrators, appointment, language and governing law.
I confirm whether each relevant country is a party to the New York Convention.
I know that governing law and the seat of arbitration are separate choices.
I prefer security I can call, such as a letter of credit, over a judgment I must chase.
I never assume a limitation period; I get counsel's view in writing.
I have the dispute clause reviewed for each new counterparty, not copied.
head: Field checklist
speak: Choose the final forum when you sign, not when you fight, and choose it by one question: if I win, can I collect where the other side's money is? Courts are public, appealable, and you get the judge assigned. Arbitration is private, decided by arbitrators the parties help choose, usually final, and not reliably cheaper. The big difference across borders is enforcement. Under the 1958 New York Convention, member countries agree to recognise each other's arbitral awards on narrow grounds, while foreign court judgments often need a fresh proceeding. So a good arbitration clause names the seat, the rules, how many arbitrators and how they are appointed, the language and the governing law. Then remember the clock. Every system sets limitation periods, often running from discovery with a long-stop behind them. Never assume a number. Get counsel's view in writing, in each jurisdiction.
terms: Seat of arbitration — the legal home of an arbitration, which decides which country's courts supervise it and hear any challenge to the award.
New York Convention — the 1958 treaty under which member countries agree to recognise and enforce arbitral awards made in other member countries, on limited grounds of refusal.
Separability — the principle that an arbitration clause is treated as a separate agreement from the contract that contains it.

hostile.q: Your clause says disputes go to your home courts. My company has no assets in your country. What exactly do you think you can enforce?
hostile.a: You are right that a home-court judgment would need recognition where your assets are, and I would rather not rely on that. That is why I am proposing to replace the clause with arbitration under named institutional rules, seated in a neutral country that recognises foreign awards, with three arbitrators and English as the language. It protects you as much as me: both of us get a decision that travels. And I will want a parent guarantee or a letter of credit sized to the contract, so that neither of us has to enforce anything at all.

title: Valuing a Contractor's Delay Claim, Step by Step
summary: A contractor claims 90 days of delay and 1,350,000 dollars. Quincy takes the claim apart line by line: entitlement to time, the daily rate for prolongation, disruption, overhead and profit, and the owner's own counter-claim. The result is a defensible range and a settlement number with its working shown.
body:
A delay claim is not one number. It is a stack of separate claims, each needing its own proof of time and its own proof of cost, and most of the value of a negotiation comes from separating them.

Recall

Q. What is the seat of an arbitration?

A. Its legal home, which decides which country's courts supervise the arbitration and hear any challenge to the award. It is a separate choice from the governing law of the contract.

Q. What are liquidated damages?

A. A fixed amount per day or week, agreed in the contract, that the contractor pays the owner for late completion, in place of proving actual loss. Whether a given rate is enforceable depends on the governing law.

Q. Why should a developer track relationships with institutions, not only brokers?

A. Because banks, pension funds, development agencies and public landowners bring repeat opportunities over years, and those relationships are built by delivering on small commitments long before a deal appears.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, when a contractor's claim lands on your desk, it will usually arrive as a single impressive total with a thick appendix. The temptation is to negotiate the total: they ask 1,350,000 dollars, you offer half, you meet somewhere. That wastes money in both directions. Valuing the claim component by component tells you what is genuinely owed, what is arguable and what is padding, and it gives you a number you can explain to your lender, your investors and, if necessary, an arbitrator. All figures here are hypothetical.

The claim as submitted

A contractor on a 24-month residential project claims an extension of 90 days and 1,350,000 dollars, made up of:

  • Extended site overheads, called prolongation: 90 days at 9,000 dollars a day, 810,000 dollars.
  • Head office overhead: 90 days at 2,500 dollars a day, 225,000 dollars.
  • Disruption and lost productivity on the structure: 200,000 dollars.
  • Profit at 10 percent on the above: 115,000 dollars, rounded.

Total 1,350,000 dollars. The stated causes are late design information from the owner's architect and a late utility connection.

Step 1: entitlement to time

First the time, because cost follows time. Your scheduler, Petra's seat, runs a time impact analysis: inserting each delay event into the schedule as it stood just before the event and measuring the effect on completion. Suppose it shows late design information caused 50 days of critical delay, the utility connection 30 days, but the utility delay ran in parallel with 30 days the contractor caused itself through a shortage of formwork crews. Delays running at the same time from both sides are called concurrent delay, and how they are treated depends on the contract and the governing law. Assume your contract gives the contractor time, but not money, for concurrent periods.

So: 50 days compensable, meaning time and money. 30 days excusable but not compensable, meaning time only. The contractor's own 10 remaining claimed days are not supported. Extension of time: 80 days. Compensable days: 50.

Say that out loud now.

Cost follows time. First prove which days, then price the days.

Step 2: the daily rate for prolongation

The claimed 9,000 dollars a day for site overheads must be tested against the contractor's actual time-related costs: site management salaries, site accommodation, equipment on hire, temporary utilities, insurance. Suppose the records show 7,000 dollars a day of genuinely time-related cost during the delay period, because some claimed items, such as the tower crane, had already left site. Prolongation: 50 days times 7,000 dollars equals 350,000 dollars.

Step 3: head office overhead

Head office overhead claims are commonly calculated by a formula that spreads the contractor's annual overhead across its turnover. They are contested because a contractor may not have actually lost other work. Suppose your contract allows head office overhead only with evidence that it was genuinely unrecovered. The contractor's accounts support 1,500 dollars a day. Head office: 50 days times 1,500 dollars equals 75,000 dollars, and you mark it as arguable.

Step 4: disruption

Disruption is loss of productivity, the same work taking more labour hours, rather than delay to completion. The strongest method compares productivity in an unaffected period with the affected period, from the contractor's own labour records. Suppose those records support 120,000 dollars of the 200,000 claimed, and the remainder is a percentage applied without evidence. Disruption: 120,000 dollars.

Step 5: profit, and the owner's side

Whether profit is recoverable on delay costs depends on the contract. Suppose it allows 5 percent on compensable delay costs, not 10. On 350,000 plus 75,000 plus 120,000, which is 545,000 dollars, profit is 27,250 dollars. Contractor's supported total: about 572,000 dollars.

Now the owner's side. The contractor finished 90 days late but is entitled to 80 days of extension. The remaining 10 days are its own. If the contract sets liquidated damages at 5,000 dollars a day, the owner may deduct 50,000 dollars, subject to the governing law. Net to the contractor: about 522,000 dollars.

Step 6: the range and the number

Your valuation is a range, not a point. Low case, excluding the arguable head office overhead: 572,000 less 75,000 less 3,750 of profit on it, about 493,000 dollars gross, 443,000 dollars net of liquidated damages. High case, accepting all supported items: about 522,000 dollars net. The claim was 1,350,000 dollars. A settlement around 480,000 to 520,000 dollars has its working shown, line by line, and can be defended to anyone.

The summary table

Put the whole valuation on one page before any meeting. Read it aloud once, because if you cannot say each line in a sentence, you do not yet understand it well enough to negotiate it.

ItemClaimed (dollars)Supported (dollars)
Prolongation810,000350,000
Head office overhead225,00075,000, arguable
Disruption200,000120,000
Profit115,00027,250
Liquidated damages to ownernoneminus 50,000
Net1,350,000about 522,000

Notice where the gap comes from. More than half of the reduction is in prolongation, and most of that is the days, not the rate: 90 claimed against 50 compensable. That tells you where the negotiation will be fought. If the contractor can show you that the utility delay was not concurrent with its own formwork shortage, 30 days move from time-only to compensable, and the high case rises by about 270,000 dollars once overhead and profit are added. That single schedule question is worth more than every other line combined, so that is where you spend your expert's time.

What to ask the contractor for

Before any settlement meeting, request in writing: the native schedule files, not only printed bar charts; the daily site diaries and labour returns for the delay period; payroll for site staff; hire invoices with on-hire and off-hire dates; the audited accounts behind the head office rate; and every notice it sent under the contract's claims clause, with dates. A contractor with a genuine claim will produce these quickly. One that delays production is telling you something about the claim.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is negotiating the total rather than the components, so you overpay for padding or underpay a genuine claim and provoke an arbitration you will lose. The control is a written valuation with separate entitlement to time, a tested daily rate, evidenced disruption, the contract's own profit rule and your counter-claims, prepared by a quantity surveyor and a scheduler together.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner accepts the contractor's daily rate because it looks precise. A precise number is not an evidenced number. Ask for the payroll, the hire invoices and the dates each resource arrived and left.

Callback

In Week 50, Petra taught critical path logic and float ownership. Everything in Step 1 rests on that lesson: delay that consumes float without moving completion is not compensable delay, and a schedule without sound logic cannot prove anything to a tribunal.

Recap

A 1,350,000 dollar claim became a defensible 443,000 to 522,000 dollar range by proving time first, testing the daily rate against records, demanding evidence for disruption, applying the contract's own profit rule and netting the owner's liquidated damages. Professional sign-off required: quantity surveyor and forensic scheduler, with counsel on the contract terms.

Next: LEX in The Room: the mediation day, what to say, what never to say and when to stay silent.
checklist: I separate every claim into time, prolongation, overhead, disruption and profit.
I prove entitlement to time with a time impact analysis before pricing any cost.
I split delay into compensable, excusable and the contractor's own.
I test every daily rate against payroll, hire invoices and resource dates.
I accept disruption only with productivity evidence from the contractor's own records.
I apply the contract's profit rule, not the contractor's.
I net my own counter-claims, such as liquidated damages, before settling.
I state my valuation as a range with each line's working shown.
head: Field checklist
speak: A delay claim is a stack of separate claims, and you negotiate the stack, not the total. In the example, a contractor asked 1,350,000 dollars for 90 days. First prove time: the time impact analysis gave 50 days compensable, 30 days time only because of concurrent delay, and 10 days that were the contractor's own. Then price the days: actual site overheads were 7,000 dollars a day, not 9,000, so 350,000 dollars. Head office overhead was arguable at 75,000. Disruption had evidence for 120,000 of 200,000. The contract allowed 5 percent profit, not 10. That gives about 572,000 dollars. Then net the owner's side: 10 late days at 5,000 dollars of liquidated damages. The result is a range of roughly 443,000 to 522,000 dollars, every line evidenced. That is a number you can defend to a lender, an investor or an arbitrator.
terms: Prolongation — the time-related site costs a contractor incurs because the job lasts longer than planned.
Concurrent delay — delay caused by both parties during the same period, whose treatment depends on the contract and governing law.
Disruption — loss of productivity, where the same work takes more labour or plant, as distinct from delay to completion.

hostile.q: We have 90 days of delay and a thick claim. You are offering a third. Are you just negotiating?
hostile.a: No. Every line of my number has its working attached. Your 90 days becomes 80 days of extension, of which 50 carry money, on our time impact analysis, which I will share. Your payroll and hire records support 7,000 dollars a day on site, not 9,000, and your labour records support 120,000 dollars of disruption. Show me evidence for the rest and I will move. Without it, I will ask the independent expert in our contract to decide.

title: The Mediation Day
summary: A mediation is a day of short joint sessions and long private ones, where a neutral tests each side's case and carries offers between rooms. LEX walks through the day: what to say in the opening, what never to say, the question behind the mediator's questions, when to stay silent, and how to hold your state when the first offer is insulting.
body:
At a mediation you are not there to win the argument. You are there to reach the best settlement available that day, and to leave with a signed term sheet or a clear reason why not.

Recall

Q. In valuing a delay claim, why do you prove time before pricing cost?

A. Because cost follows time. Only days that are compensable under the contract carry money, so the time impact analysis decides how many days the daily rate is multiplied by.

Q. What is a letter of credit used for in construction?

A. As security: a bank's promise to pay a named beneficiary on presentation of stated documents, which lets the owner or contractor call money without first winning a dispute.

Q. What makes a landowner relationship durable?

A. Doing what you said, when you said, on small matters first, and being transparent about how the land's value is assessed, because landowners talk to each other.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, most construction disputes that reach the upper rungs of the ladder settle, and many settle at or shortly after a mediation. The day itself is a performance under pressure, often lasting 10 or 12 hours, with an unfamiliar structure. The developer who understands that structure keeps his composure, protects his position and closes. The one who does not either gives too much late in the evening or walks out on a settlement better than his trial outcome.

The scene

Hypothetical. You claim 1,800,000 dollars from a contractor and its subcontractor for a defective envelope. You have a written valuation, Roman's method from Day 3, with a walk-away of 900,000 dollars and authority to settle above it. You arrive at 9 in the morning with your lawyer. The mediator, an experienced construction lawyer, holds a short joint session, then puts each side in its own room. For most of the day she moves between rooms. Anything you tell her in private stays private unless you authorise her to pass it on.

The opening: the lines to say

If you speak in the joint session, keep it short and addressed to the decision-makers across the table, not to their lawyers.

  • "We want this building fixed and this matter closed today if we can."
  • "Our consultant's report and our costings are in the bundle. We are happy to walk through any part of them."
  • "I respect that your team has worked hard on this job. This is about who pays for a defect, not about anyone's character."
  • "We have authority to settle today."

Then stop. Let your lawyer handle the law.

The lines never to say

  • Your walk-away number, ever, to anyone outside your own room, including the mediator unless you have decided to use it.
  • "We will never accept less than the full amount." It locks you in, and both sides know it is not true.
  • Personal attacks on the other side's people. They harden the room and give the mediator nothing to work with.
  • Anything about your own cash position, your lender's patience or your investors' questions. Those are pressure points, and you have just handed them over.

Say that out loud now.

I came to settle today. I will not reveal my floor, and I will not attack their people.

The question behind the question

In private session the mediator will ask what sound like neutral questions. Hear what each one is really asking.

  • "How confident are you on liability?" She is testing whether you have priced the risk of losing.
  • "What would a tribunal really award on the disruption items?" She is inviting you to discount your own claim before the other side does.
  • "How long can you carry this?" She is gauging your patience and cost of delay.
  • "What would it take to close today?" She is asking for movement, not your bottom line. Answer with a move, not a number you cannot leave.

Answer honestly but strategically. Acknowledge real weaknesses in private; she will not believe a case with none, and conceding the weak point buys credibility for the strong ones.

When to stay silent

Three moments. When the mediator delivers the other side's first offer: hear it, write it down, and say nothing for a while. When she pushes for a response at the end of a long session: say you will take ten minutes with your lawyer. And after you make an offer: stop talking. Explaining an offer after making it signals doubt and invites a lower counter.

Holding your state

The first offer will often look insulting, perhaps 200,000 dollars against your 1,800,000. That is normal theatre, not a signal. Your valuation is your anchor against it. Decide in advance the size of your first two moves, so that you are executing a plan rather than reacting. Eat properly, drink water and take a short walk outside at midday. Late in the day, fatigue, not argument, drives bad decisions; the developer who has managed his energy has an advantage at 7 in the evening. If you use a slow-breathing drill, do it seated in your own room, never while driving home. Check that with your doctor if you have any health condition.

A worked sequence, hypothetical. Their opening 200,000 dollars, your move to 1,500,000; their 450,000, your 1,250,000; their 650,000, your 1,100,000. The mediator asks if there is a number that closes today. You authorise her to explore 950,000 dollars on a without-prejudice basis, meaning a settlement discussion that cannot later be used as an admission; check how that protection applies in your jurisdiction. They come back at 900,000 dollars with payment in 30 days. You are at your walk-away, with a known timetable, and counsel confirms it beats the fight. You accept, subject to a signed term sheet before anyone leaves.

The night before

Preparation decides the day. The evening before, with your lawyer, agree four things in writing and keep them in your own folder, never in the shared bundle. First, the valuation: the expected value and the walk-away, and the reasons for each. Second, the non-money terms you care about, such as the contractor returning to repair rather than paying cash, a warranty extension, or confidentiality. Non-money terms are often where a stuck negotiation unlocks, because they cost the other side less than they are worth to you. Third, who in the room has authority, and up to what amount; if your investors or lender must approve, know how to reach them that evening. Fourth, your plan if there is no deal: the next rung of the ladder and its timetable.

Then sleep. A shift worker's instinct is to push through a long day on caffeine. Plan the caffeine instead, as Kema taught in Week 4: enough early to be sharp, little after mid-afternoon so the evening decisions are not made on a crash.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is agreeing in principle at 9 in the evening and leaving without signed terms, so the deal unravels in drafting. The control is to bring a draft settlement term sheet in the morning, with blanks for amount and dates, covering payment timing, releases, confidentiality, costs and what happens to any liens, and to sign it in the room.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner treats the mediator as a judge to be persuaded. She decides nothing. Persuade her that your valuation is realistic, so she carries that view to the other room, and let her do the rest.

Callback

In Week 6, Kema taught the three-part answer to a hostile question: acknowledge, bridge, answer. In private session the mediator's hardest questions deserve the same structure. Acknowledge the weakness she has found, bridge to the evidence, answer with a move.

Recap

A mediation is a structured day of joint and private sessions. Open briefly with intent to settle and authority to do so. Never reveal your floor, your cash position or contempt. Hear the question behind each question. Stay silent after offers. Manage your energy. Sign the term sheet before leaving. Professional sign-off required: dispute counsel on the settlement terms.

Next: Kema's Week 81 review: six questions, a Red Pen dispute clause and the two-minute boardroom drill.
checklist: I bring a written valuation with a walk-away and settlement authority.
I open briefly, with intent to settle, and leave the law to counsel.
I never disclose my floor, my cash position or my lender's patience.
I plan the size of my first two moves before the day starts.
I stay silent after hearing an offer and after making one.
I manage food, water and breaks so fatigue does not decide.
I bring a draft settlement term sheet and sign it before leaving.
head: Field checklist
speak: At a mediation you are not there to win the argument; you are there to reach the best settlement available that day. The day is a short joint session, then long private ones, with a mediator carrying offers between rooms. She decides nothing. Open briefly: we want this fixed and closed today, our evidence is in the bundle, and we have authority to settle. Never reveal your walk-away, your cash position or your lender's patience, and never attack their people. Hear the question behind her questions: how confident are you is really, have you priced losing. Admit real weaknesses privately; it buys credibility. Stay silent after you hear an offer and after you make one. Plan your first two moves in advance, manage your energy, because fatigue decides more than argument. And never leave without a signed term sheet.
terms: Mediation — a structured negotiation in which a neutral helps the parties reach their own settlement but has no power to decide.
Private session — a confidential meeting between the mediator and one side, also called a caucus, whose contents stay private unless authorised.
Without prejudice — a label on settlement discussions intended to stop them being used later as an admission, whose effect depends on the governing law.

hostile.q: Mediator, in private: you say your claim is 1,800,000 dollars. Be honest with me. What would you take to walk out of here today?
hostile.a: Honestly, our valuation, discounted for the risk on the disruption items and for two more years of process, is well below 1,800,000 dollars, and I accept the disruption evidence is thinner than the rest. I am not going to give you a floor. What I will authorise you to say is that we can move further if they come above half a million and agree to pay within 30 days.

role: Chief of staff and learning coach
title: Week 81 Review: Ladders, Clocks, Forums and the Mediation Day
summary: Six questions on the dispute ladder, the two clocks, the expected value of a claim, arbitration versus courts, valuing a delay claim and the mediation day. Then a Red Pen drill on a hypothetical dispute clause with planted defects, and the two-minute boardroom drill.
body:
This week came down to one sentence: a dispute is a business problem with a legal clock attached, so design the ladder before you need it, watch both clocks, price every claim as an investment, and choose a forum whose decision you can collect.

Recall

Q. What is a time impact analysis?

A. A scheduling method that inserts a delay event into the schedule as it stood just before the event and measures the effect on completion, used to prove entitlement to extra time.

Q. What is Monte Carlo contingency?

A. Contingency sized by simulating the project's cost or schedule many times with each risk drawn from its range, then reading the amount needed for a chosen confidence level, such as 80 percent.

Q. What is cultural intelligence in stakeholder work?

A. The ability to read and adapt to different norms on hierarchy, directness, time and relationships, so that your message lands as intended with authorities, communities and partners.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, if you can answer these six questions aloud without notes, you can sit with a construction lawyer and discuss a dispute as the client who directs the work, not the client who pays for it. Answer each before reading the answer.

The six questions

Question 1. Name the rungs of a dispute ladder and say why each needs a fixed time limit.

Answer: Negotiation, executive escalation, a dispute board or expert, mediation, then arbitration or litigation. Fixed limits stop any rung being used to stall and push unresolved issues up promptly.

Question 2. What are the two clocks on every claim?

Answer: The contractual time bar for giving notice, which can be short and defeats a claim before the law is involved, and the legal limitation period for starting proceedings, which varies by system and claim type and must be verified.

Question 3. What is a standstill agreement and when do you need one?

Answer: A contract pausing a limitation period for a defined time so talks can continue without loss of rights. You need one before any limitation date comes close while settlement talks are still running.

Question 4. How do you value a claim?

Answer: Probability of success times the realistic award, plus expected cost recovery, discounted for time, adjusted for collection risk, less fees. Then add the costs no invoice shows: locked cash, delay, financing friction and management time.

Question 5. What decides the choice between arbitration and court for a cross-border contract?

Answer: Above all, enforcement: whether you can collect where the counterparty's assets are. Arbitral awards between parties to the New York Convention usually travel more easily than court judgments; verify each country's status.

Question 6. In valuing a delay claim, what is the order of work?

Answer: Prove entitlement to time first, splitting compensable, excusable and the contractor's own delay; then test the daily rate against records; then evidence disruption; apply the contract's profit rule; and net your counter-claims.

Say that out loud now.

Recap of the week

LEX built the dispute ladder and the two clocks. Ford and Cole took a composite envelope claim lost because talks ran past the notice periods and the limitation period, giving Rule 81. Roman priced disputes as investments and showed what delay does to IRR. LEX compared arbitration and courts, explained the seat and the New York Convention, and compared Canada and Guyana conceptually. Quincy reduced a 1,350,000 dollar delay claim to a defensible range. LEX ran the mediation day.

The Red Pen

Read this hypothetical dispute clause and find the defects before reading on.

Clause 22. Disputes. 22.1 The parties shall attempt to resolve any dispute amicably. 22.2 Failing agreement, either party may refer the dispute to arbitration in a suitable location under appropriate rules. 22.3 Pending resolution, the Owner may withhold all payments under this Contract. 22.4 Claims by the Contractor shall be notified within 7 days of the event; claims by the Owner may be notified at any time. 22.5 This clause is without prejudice to either party's right to commence proceedings in any court.

The defects. First, clause 22.1 sets no time limit and no escalation step, so amicable talks can run indefinitely while the limitation clock runs. Second, clause 22.2 names no seat, no rules, no number of arbitrators, no appointing method and no language; a clause this vague may fail and force the parties to litigate about where to litigate. Third, clause 22.3 lets the owner withhold all payment, not only disputed amounts, which invites the contractor to stop work and may be unenforceable or penalised by payment legislation in some places; verify that against the primary source. Fourth, clause 22.4 is lopsided: a 7-day notice for the contractor and none for the owner may be read against the owner, and a tribunal may be unsympathetic to it. Fifth, clause 22.5 contradicts 22.2 by preserving court proceedings, so both sides can race to different forums. Sixth, there is no duty to keep working, no independent expert or board, and no governing law.

The rewrite in outline: negotiation within 14 days, executive escalation within 14 more, a named independent expert for technical disputes deciding within 28 days, mediation, and then arbitration with seat, rules, three arbitrators, appointment, English and governing law stated; work continues and undisputed sums are paid throughout; notice periods are reasonable and apply to both sides.

The boardroom drill

Explain the week in two minutes, as if to an investor who asks, "What happens if we end up in a fight with the contractor?" Record it, then compare with this model.

Model answer: "First, the contract is built to stop a fight becoming expensive. Disagreements go up a ladder with fixed time limits: project managers, then executives, then an independent expert who knows the job, then mediation, and only then arbitration. Work continues and undisputed sums are paid throughout, so the site does not stop. Second, I watch two clocks on every claim, the contract's notice deadlines and the legal limitation period, and I sign a standstill agreement rather than let talks run past either. Third, I value every claim as an investment: chance of winning, realistic award, fees, time and whether they can pay. That tells me when to settle. Fourth, our final forum is arbitration seated in a neutral country, because an award is easier to enforce where a foreign contractor's assets are. Your exposure is in the contingency and a reserve, and I report any material claim to you and the lender the week it arises."

Score yourself. Did you lead with the bottom line? Did you name both clocks? Did you describe valuation as probability, quantum, time and collection rather than face amount? Did you finish inside two minutes? If not, record it again tomorrow.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk this week is confusing being right with winning. A right claim without notice, records, a valuation and an enforceable forum can be worth nothing. The control is procedure: a claims register, formal notices, written valuations and a dispute clause reviewed by counsel before signing.

The beginner's mistake

Leaving the dispute clause to the end of the negotiation, as boilerplate. It is the clause that decides whether every other clause can be enforced.

Callback

In Week 78, LEX taught risk allocation: indemnities, limits of liability and consequential loss. Those clauses decide what a claim is worth. This week's clauses decide whether you can ever collect it. Read the two weeks together whenever you review a contract.

Recap

Ladders filter disagreements cheaply. Two clocks can kill strong claims. Claims are priced as investments. The forum is chosen for enforcement. Delay claims are valued component by component. Mediation is won by preparation, silence and a signed term sheet. Rule 81 keeps the calendar from deciding your case.

head: The six questions
speak: Here is the week in a minute. A dispute is a business problem with a legal clock attached. Build a dispute ladder into the contract: project managers, executives, an independent expert or board, mediation, and only then arbitration or court, each with fixed time limits, while work continues and undisputed sums are paid. Watch two clocks: the contract's notice deadlines and the legal limitation period, and sign a standstill agreement before talks run past either. That is Rule 81. Value every claim as an investment: chance of winning times the realistic award, less fees, discounted for time and for whether they can pay. Choose the final forum for enforcement; arbitral awards usually travel better under the New York Convention. Value delay claims component by component, time first. And at mediation, prepare, stay silent after offers, and sign the term sheet before you leave.
terms: Pathological clause — a dispute resolution clause so vague or contradictory that it cannot operate without a further dispute about its meaning.
Payment legislation — statutes in some jurisdictions that regulate payment timing in construction contracts and limit the withholding of payment; verify locally.
Term sheet — a short signed summary of the agreed settlement terms, used to bind the main points before full documents are drafted.

hostile.q: Your contract sends disputes to arbitration. Isn't that just paying for a private judge on top of the lawyers?
hostile.a: It can be, and I do not assume it is cheaper. I chose it for two reasons. Our contractor's assets are abroad, and an award is usually far easier to enforce there than a home-court judgment. And we choose arbitrators who understand construction. Most disputes should never reach it: the ladder has an independent expert who decides technical issues in 28 days for a small fixed fee, and that is where I expect almost everything to end.
